claims.claim: The primary USGS field procedure for determining dissolved oxygen is the luminescence-based (optical) sensor, which is more robust in the field, is not flow dependent, and gives higher quality data than amperometric sensors especially at low DO concentrations below 2 milligrams per liter.
claims.quote:
are not
flow dependent, and are generally easier to use while provid-
ing higher quality data, especially at low DO concentrations
(<2 milligrams per liter [mg/L]).

claims.claim: Spectrophotometric (colorimetric) instrumental methods can be used to report dissolved-oxygen concentrations from about 2.0 mg/L down to as little as 0.025 mg/L.

can
be used to report DO concentrations from about 2.0 mg/L to
as little as 0.025 mg/L.

claims.claim: Noninstrumental colorimetric methods for visually determining dissolved-oxygen concentrations may be used for quick reconnaissance or an accuracy check but must not be used to report DO concentrations.
claims.quote:
Noninstrumental colorimetric methods that are available for
visually determining DO concentrations should not be used to
report DO concentrations.

claims.claim: Standard USGS practice no longer sanctions onsite Winkler (iodometric) titrations or the transport of field samples offsite for dissolved-oxygen determination by the Winkler method.
claims.quote:
Standard USGS practice
no longer sanctions onsite Winkler titrations or the transport
of field samples offsite for DO determination by the Winkler
method.

claims.claim: The concentration of dissolved oxygen in water is affected by many factors, including ambient temperature, atmospheric pressure, and ion activity (the ionic strength of the water body).
claims.quote:
The concentration of DO in water is affected by many
factors, including ambient temperature, atmospheric pressure,
and ion activity (ionic strength of the water body).

claims.claim: Dissolved oxygen is defined as molecular oxygen (oxygen gas) dissolved in water.
claims.quote:
DISSOLVED OXYGEN: Molecular oxygen (oxygen gas)
dissolved in water.

claims.claim: Sources of dissolved oxygen in water include atmospheric aeration and the photosynthetic activities of aquatic plants.
claims.quote:
Sources

synthetic activities of aquatic plants.

claims.quote:
Sinks of DO in water
include respiration, aerobic decomposition processes, ammo-
nia nitrification, and other chemical and biological reactions.

claims.claim: Dissolved oxygen is necessary for the survival and growth of many aquatic organisms and is used as an indicator of the health and geochemical quality of surface-water and groundwater systems; the manual gives no numeric concentration for that role.
claims.quote:
The presence of DO in aquatic systems is necessary for the
survival and growth of many aquatic organisms and is used as
an indicator of the health and geochemical quality

claims.claim: Optical sensors have replaced the amperometric (Clark cell) sensor, and barring project-specific requirements optical sensors should be considered the standard USGS field method.
claims.quote:
Optical sensors have replaced
the amperometric type of sensor.

claims.claim: The iodometric (Winkler) method is no longer used by the USGS for routine field measurement of dissolved oxygen but remains an acceptable method for verifying results obtained with other methods.
claims.quote:

Section 2.0 Optical (Luminescence) Sensor Method / Technical Note 1 — "Some characteristics of the optical DO method"

claims.claim: The optical dissolved-oxygen sensor does not consume oxygen at the sensor-water interface and is not dependent on water flow, so no stirring mechanism is required at sites with slowly flowing or still water.

There are no known sources of interference to the luminescence method in natural aquatic systems; optical sensors measure accurately in the presence of hydrogen sulfide and in fresh, brackish, and mildly contaminated waters, but contact with organic solvents can compromise sensor integrity or performance.
claims.quote:
Optical sensors will measure accurately in the pres-
ence of hydrogen sulfide (H2S) and also when deployed
in fresh, brackish, and mildly contaminated waters.

claims.claim: The optical sensor contains no anode or cathode to service and uses no electrolyte solution, membranes, or O-rings.
claims.quote:
The optical sensor contains no anode or cathode to
service, and uses no electrolyte solution, membranes,
or O-rings.

claims.claim: Manufacturers generally recommend annual to biannual replacement of the luminophore-containing module, and sensors should be calibrated or undergo a calibration check after module replacement.
claims.quote:
Manufacturers generally recommend annual to bian-
nual replacement of the luminophore-containing
module (also called “lumiphore”).

claims.claim: In a luminescence dissolved-oxygen sensor an LED excites a luminescent-dye molecule and oxygen quenches the fluorescence, so higher DO concentrations produce greater quenching and a decreased fluorescence response, with the strongest detector signal at the lowest DO concentrations.
claims.quote:
Higher DO concentrations result in greater quench-
ing and a decreased fluorescence response. The signal to the
fluorescence detector is greatest at lowest DO concentrations.

claims.claim: The main goal of the one-point DO calibration is to create a 100-percent saturated oxygen environment in which the DO sensor and its thermistor are at the same temperature, achieved either by calibration in air (Procedure 1) or calibration in air-saturated water (Procedure 2).

The main goal of the one-point

oxygen environment in which the DO sensor and its thermistor
are at the same temperature.

(2) oxygen concentrations

ment sensors to prevent possible interference of the

salinity corrections should not be necessary for

claims.claim: The solubility of oxygen in water depends on the temperature and ionic strength of the water: the higher the atmospheric pressure at the water surface and the lower the temperature and conductivity of the water, the more oxygen will be dissolved.
claims.quote:
The higher the
atmospheric pressure on the water’s surface and the lower the
temperature and conductivity of the water, the more oxygen
will be dissolved in the water.

claims.claim: Degassing, mineral precipitation, and other chemical, physical, and biological reactions can cause the dissolved-oxygen concentration of a water sample to change substantially within minutes after collection, especially for water originally isolated from the atmosphere such as groundwater or deep lake water.
claims.quote:
other chemical,
physical, and biological reactions can cause the DO concentra-
tion of a water sample to change substantially within minutes
after sample collection

claims.claim: The solubility of oxygen in water decreases as salinity increases, and correction factors for salinity are typically applied after measuring DO for single-point samples.
claims.quote:
The solubility of oxygen in water decreases as salinity
increases. Correction factors for salinity typically are applied
after measuring DO for single-point samples

claims.claim: Standard determinations of dissolved oxygen in riverine surface water represent the cross-sectional median or mean DO concentration at the time of observation.
claims.quote:
Standard determinations of DO in riverine surface water
represent the cross-sectional median or mean DO concentra-
tion at the time of observation.

chunks.locator: Section 2.3.1 Surface Water — "cross-sectional DO variation less than 0.5 mg/L"

claims.claim: Measuring the dissolved-oxygen concentration at one distinct point in a stream cross section is valid only for flowing water whose cross-sectional DO variation is less than 0.5 mg/L, and discerning that variation requires a reconnaissance cross-section measurement.
claims.quote:
Measuring the DO concentration at one distinct point in
a cross section is valid only for flowing water with a cross-
sectional DO variation less than 0.5 mg/L.

claims.claim: Dissolved oxygen must not be measured in or directly below sections with turbulent flow, in still water, or from the bank, unless those conditions represent most of the stream reach or are required to fulfill project objectives.
claims.quote:
Do not measure DO in or directly below sections with
turbulent flow, in still water, or from the bank unless these
conditions represent most of the stream reach

claims.claim: If the anticipated dissolved-oxygen concentration is less than 1.0 mg/L, spectrophotometric methods are required to develop an instrument-specific rating before measurements made with a field instrument can be reported.
claims.quote:
If the anticipated DO concentration is less than 1.0 mg/L,
use of spectrophotometric methods (section 3.0) is required
to develop an instrument-specific rating

claims.claim: An instrument-specific rating should consist of at least five measurements made as nearly simultaneously as possible with the optical instrument and the spectrophotometric method, and the medians of those measurements should agree within 0.03 mg/L.
claims.quote:
measurements made as nearly
simultaneously as possible with the optical instrument and
the spectrophotometric method. When compared, the median
of these measurements should agree within 0.03 mg/L.

chunks.locator: Section 2.3.1, page break — "metric methods. The instrument-specific rating" (overlap text only)
Section 2.3.1 Surface Water, measurement steps — "DO must be measured in situ"

claims.claim: Once an instrument-specific rating has been developed, an optical DO instrument may be used to report dissolved-oxygen concentrations greater than 0.03 mg/L.
claims.quote:
Once an instrument-specific rating has been developed, an
optical DO instrument may be used to report DO concentra-
tions greater than 0.03 mg/L.

claims.claim: Dissolved oxygen must be measured in situ and never in subsamples taken from a sample splitter or other vessel, because the chemistry of derived samples changes quickly and such measurements are not representative.
claims.quote:
DO must be measured in situ. Never measure DO in
subsamples from a sample splitter or other vessel; DO
measurements will not be representative

claims.claim: The DO and temperature sensors are immersed directly into the water body and allowed to equilibrate to the water temperature for no less than 60 seconds.
claims.quote:
allow the sensors to equilibrate to the
water temperature (no less than 60 seconds).

claims.claim: After the instrument reading has stabilized to within ±0.2 mg/L the median DO concentration is recorded, and in still water the median of three or more sequential values is recorded.
claims.quote:
The reading should stabilize to within ±0.2
mg/L.
• In still water, record the median of three or more
sequential values.

claims.claim: For Equal Discharge Increment sampling the mean value of all subsections measured is recorded (or the median at the centroid of flow if there is only one vertical section), and for Equal Width Increment sampling the mean or median of all subsections is recorded.
claims.quote:
Equal Discharge Increment (EDI)—Record the mean
value of all subsections measured.

claims.claim: Spectrophotometric methods for determining dissolved-oxygen concentration generally are not approved by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency for regulatory assessments.
claims.quote:
spectrophotometric methods for determining DO concentration
generally are not approved by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency for
regulatory assessments.

claims.claim: In a flowing stream too deep or swift to wade, a weighted DO sensor is lowered from a bridge, cableway, or boat, and the weight must not be attached directly to the sensors or sensor cables.
claims.quote:
Do not attach the weight directly to the sensors
or sensor cables to avoid damaging the sensors or
sensor cables.

claims.claim: In lakes and reservoirs dissolved oxygen is measured at a series of specific depths to determine a vertical profile at each location of interest, and in still-water conditions at multiple depths at several points in the cross section.
claims.quote:
Lakes and reservoirs—Measure DO at a series of
specific depths to determine a vertical profile at each
location of interest.

chunks.locator: Section 2.3.2 Groundwater — "standing water must be evacuated from the well"

claims.claim: Before the concentration of dissolved oxygen in groundwater can be determined, standing water must be evacuated from the well so that the measurement is representative of formation-water concentration; an adequate well purge ensures the flow of freshwater from the aquifer formation into the well.
claims.quote:
standing water must be evacuated from the well
to ensure that measurements of DO concentration in the well
will be representative of formation-water concentration.

claims.claim: A bailed sample is not recommended for dissolved-oxygen measurement because the field sample-decanting process exposes the sample to the atmosphere, and the same applies to any sampling device from which the sample contacts air during transfer.
claims.quote:
A bailed sample, for
example, is not recommended for DO measurement because
the field sample-decanting process exposes the sample to the
atmosphere

claims.claim: Project data-quality requirements, site characteristics, and equipment availability dictate whether groundwater DO measurements are made in situ (downhole) or ex situ above land surface by the inline-flow procedure, and whether optical or spectrophotometric methods are used.
claims.quote:
(1) measurements will be made in situ (DO measured down-
hole) or ex situ (DO measured above land surface, the inline-
flow procedure)
